title: The Monarchy's Quiet Constitutional Role
label: 16 September 2026 · Lord Young on constitutional safeguards
summary: Lord Young of Old Windsor, former principal private secretary to the sovereign, gave the Constitution Committee a first-hand account of how the monarchy works in practice. He stressed the centrality of the private weekly audience between monarch and Prime Minister, the importance of confidentiality, and the reserve powers that remain unused but act as a restraining influence. He described a near-crisis during Covid when Boris Johnson was seriously ill, and argued that the UK's unwritten constitution has proved adaptable, though he would welcome an updated Cabinet Manual and better public understanding.

chapters.title: The weekly audience at the heart of the constitution
chapters.takeaway: The private hour between monarch and Prime Minister is the core of the constitutional relationship, built on absolute confidentiality.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Lord Young. You worked at the palace for a long time. How would you describe the monarch's constitutional role in today's governance?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Thank you. I should declare I'm occasionally a paid consultant to the Royal Household. Let me paint a picture. I was in the room for the appointment of six Prime Ministers, or seven if you count Tony Blair's final reappointment. The core of it was the weekly audience with the Prime Minister.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It was almost always at Buckingham Palace, usually Wednesday after PMQs, around 6.15pm. The private secretary would greet the PM, spend five or ten minutes alone with them, then they'd see the Queen for an hour. Meanwhile I'd spend the most useful constitutional hour of the week downstairs with the PM's principal private secretary.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: My number one duty was to make sure there was never a gap between Head of State and Head of Government. We'd talk over a sandwich, sometimes a glass of wine. After the audience, the PM would come in and debrief. Without exception, they all walked a bit taller.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Who wouldn't cherish an hour a week with someone who won't put it on X, won't gossip, won't put it in their memoirs, and won't pursue self-interest? The sovereign has the right to be consulted, to encourage, and to warn. Encouragement might be 'How are you getting on with those things in the Queen's Speech?' A warning might be a raised eyebrow, or saying 'I was in Wigan last week and heard a different story.'

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The privacy of that meeting was extremely important.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Absolutely the crux. There's a tension between openness and the need for privacy. I dealt with Freedom of Information issues—the Royal Household wasn't officially party, but adjacent. The principle that policy formulation is protected, not just the resultant policy, is there because otherwise people can't express views candidly. Confidentiality is core.

chapters.title: Reserve powers and the restraining effect of uncertainty
chapters.takeaway: The monarch's reserve powers exist but are rarely used; the mere perception of them restrains governments.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Could there be occasions when the monarch should act as a constitutional restraint beyond that weekly hour?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. We have an unwritten constitution built on centuries of common law. It boils down to personalities. Every Government has taken the duty to be consulted seriously. But the PM also has the right to say 'Thank you, I've taken your counsel, but I'm choosing differently.' That's the compact.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: There are occasions when discretionary reserve powers could be exercised. For example, appointing a Prime Minister. Usually the sovereign appoints on the outgoing PM's advice, but if it's not obvious who can command confidence, or if the advice is questionable, the sovereign could take broader counsel. In that scenario, the outgoing PM is no longer fully authorised.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would the private secretary advise the monarch then?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: The private secretary would take soundings from the Cabinet Secretary, perhaps political leaders via the Cabinet Secretary. Another example: could a sovereign decline a request for Prorogation when a Government is about to fall? If there's been a no-confidence vote or the Cabinet has lost confidence, and the PM asks for a general election, the sovereign might decline. It's a request, not advice, because it's a reserve power.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: But if things are working well, it should never come to that. A constitutional guide would say 'No sudden moves, no surprises.' One great power of the sovereign is the perception of power—the fear they might say no. That's a restrainer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is it beneficial for the sovereign to have residual powers shrouded in opacity so they can develop in novel situations?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, I agree. Look at the alternative—a written constitution, but even then how do you spell out every eventuality? I recall a real example with Boris Johnson's permission. At the start of Covid, when he was hospitalised and believed to be near needing a ventilator, I was walking home in the rain and got a call.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: The protection officers had overheard consultants preparing to tell Carrie that her husband might go on a ventilator with a 50/50 chance. This was a real constitutional test. There's precedent for a PM dying, like Spencer Perceval or Bonar Law. But what if a PM is incommunicado indefinitely during a national crisis, with no Deputy PM?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Sitting in a bus shelter in Battersea, more people joined the call. We worked out that the Cabinet Secretary would summon the Cabinet and not let them leave until they decided who to recommend to the Queen as PM, perhaps for a set period until Boris recovered or a leadership election could be held. Someone was getting hold of Jeremy Corbyn's office, which signalled it would sign up to this plan. It never happened, but it was a good worked example of everyone coming together. It worked because of the trust we built every time one of the golden triangle changed.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: That relies on the holders caring, understanding this specialist topic, not being partisan or spad-like, and understanding the constitutional ramifications. That has always happened, but there's a risk it might not in future.

chapters.title: What if a Prime Minister refuses to go?
chapters.takeaway: Conventions around losing a confidence vote are strong, but the sovereign's reserve powers could theoretically be used in an extreme breakdown.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What if a Government lose a vote of no confidence but refuse to resign, there's no request for Prorogation, no alternative figure can command a majority, and there's deadlock?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It depends on personalities and political mood. Courts can only go so far where Parliament has primacy. If a PM refused to play ball, the sovereign might want to exercise greater power. Whether it would come to a Gough Whitlam scenario, where the sovereign dismisses a PM, would depend on events, but that reserve power is there. The fear of it has been a restrainer—even a headline implying a Minister had incurred the Palace's wrath was enough to prevent things.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is a Prime Minister refusing to resign after losing a confidence vote a real risk? That's one of our firmest conventions. Are conventions too lax—do we need to know more?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Conventions evolve. In that scenario, it's hard to see how a PM who lost confidence and refused to go would have any Cabinet left. The whole thing would crumble. A PM who could get no legislation through and had no Cabinet wouldn't last long, regardless of the sovereign.

chapters.title: Trust, transparency and the 'good faith' theory
chapters.takeaway: Confidentiality and public trust create a paradox, resolved by the monarchy's long-term, non-partisan role as head of nation.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How do you encourage public trust when the system depends on discretion and confidentiality?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: There's a paradox: how can you have trust if you don't know what's going on? The advantage of our monarchy is that government is about tomorrow's headlines, but monarchy and state are about the next five or ten years. It's about convening groups, recognising service, ensuring a broad cross-section meets the Head of State, and representing the UK globally. Over time, that feeds the feeling that the King or Queen acts in the national interest and isn't partial. That's how you square the circle.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So it's about visibility?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, certainly.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We need to speed up.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The King championed causes like climate change and architecture before becoming monarch. How does the palace manage the tension when he has to be neutral?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It's broadly accepted that as heir you can pursue interests as long as you put them aside when you take the top job. The then Prince of Wales made that clear. Remember the drumbeat: 'He'll be an interventionist King, rejecting legislation.' None of that has happened. The transition was as smooth as could be hoped.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What if a Government introduces censorship of the press? Is the monarchy the ultimate constitutional backstop, or a broken reed?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It depends. Was it a manifesto commitment? Did it pass both Houses? If a democratically elected Government with a majority pursued a manifesto commitment and it became law, it would be very difficult for a sovereign, or possibly the courts, to overturn that.

chapters.title: Who guards the constitution?
chapters.takeaway: The private secretary to the monarch is a constitutional guardian, a role that has been consistent for decades, though methods have changed.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Who guards the constitution? Is the private secretary to the monarch a guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, among many others. I see it as part of the role.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Has that changed over time?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: No. I spoke to many predecessors. The principles are remarkably consistent, certainly back to the 1950s and 1960s.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Sir Alan Lascelles wrote an anonymous letter to The Times in 1950 clarifying dissolution principles. Doesn't that show the private secretary is a constitutional guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes. Part of the role is to work out what's on the other side of the mountain. Lascelles set out principles to protect against a situation that might have arisen. Getting ahead of potential constitutional difficulty is part of the job.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Have you written any such letters?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: An anonymous letter to The Times these days would turn into a headline. Better to make someone else think it was their idea.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should the public better understand prerogative powers, or is ambiguity helpful?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Both can be true. I feel depressed when Australians know the Whitlam dismissal by heart but we don't teach our own constitution in mainstream schooling. Greater understanding at an earlier age would do a lot of good.

chapters.title: The Whitlam precedent and the limits of safeguards
chapters.takeaway: The 1975 Australian dismissal is unlikely to be repeated; the UK system relies on good faith and a functioning Cabinet, and there's no easy answer to a determined government with a majority.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The 1975 dismissal of Gough Whitlam still plays a role in Australia. What worries me is that events like Jeremy Corbyn ignoring a no-confidence vote make a similar situation in government more likely here.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Just because there's been good practice, we shouldn't assume it always will be. The sovereign is arguably the arbiter of last resort. The current Governor-General of Australia said last year she couldn't see any Governor-General acting that way today, because the right to be consulted, encourage and warn is for proper functioning of government, not political judgments. I struggle to envisage a PM acting against convention but still supported by a working Cabinet. In Whitlam's case, the whole Government had ground to a halt—people worried about getting paid.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So the constitutional safeguards are sufficient?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I don't want to sound complacent. No system is perfect. I can't see a better one, but we must stay vigilant. I'd love to see the Cabinet Manual updated—it's stuck in 2011. Every new PM should review and update it. That would give me more comfort.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: In the face of a determined Government who fully control Parliament, are there any constitutional safeguards that could withstand them?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If it's a democratically elected Government pursuing a radical manifesto commitment with a Commons majority, and it gets through the Lords, it's difficult to argue against. It's harder if more voters voted for another party but the constituency system produced a different result. Ultimately, this is a parliamentary democracy. If a democratically elected Parliament pursues its manifesto, it's difficult to call that constitutionally improper.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is that a no?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: It is what I answered.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Lord Young. That ends this public session.
